# Getting set up {#sec-setup}

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
source("_common.R")
```

R gives you a console: you type an expression and see its value. Rust doesn't come with one. You write a program in a file, compile it, and run what the compiler produces. This chapter installs the tools, builds a first program with Cargo, Rust's build tool, and then covers the syntax the next chapters rely on: variables, printing, functions, `if`, and `for` loops. The matching chapters in the Rust book are "Getting Started" and "Common Programming Concepts" [@rustbook, chaps. 1, 3].

## Installing Rust

Rust is installed and updated with `rustup` [@rustbook, sec. 1.1]. On macOS and Linux, run this in a terminal:

```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -sSf https://sh.rustup.rs | sh
```

On Windows, download and run `rustup-init.exe` from <https://rustup.rs>.

Rust also needs a *linker*, a program that joins compiled code into an executable [@rustbook, sec. 1.1]. On Windows, the installer may ask you to install the Visual Studio C++ build tools first; they provide one. On macOS, `xcode-select --install` installs one with Apple's command-line tools. On Linux, install your distribution's C compiler tools, such as Ubuntu's `build-essential`.

You'll use three tools directly: `rustc`, the compiler; `cargo`, which builds projects and manages their dependencies; and `rustup`, which keeps the other two up to date (`rustup update`). Open a new terminal after installing, so that it finds the new commands, and check that they work:

```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
rustc --version
cargo --version
```

The examples in this book use the 2024 edition of Rust, which needs Rust 1.85 or later [@rust185]. The preface lists the version used to build the book.

You'll also want an editor that understands Rust. The standard tool is rust-analyzer, which shows types and errors as you type. In VS Code and Positron, install the rust-analyzer extension.

## The Rust Playground

The closest thing Rust has to R's console is the Rust Playground, <https://play.rust-lang.org>, which compiles and runs a program in the browser. It's convenient for trying out an example from this book. For anything longer, you'll work in a project.

## A first project

The `cargo new` command creates a project:

```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
cargo new hello
cd hello
```

The project has two files that matter. Cargo also starts a Git repository and adds a `.gitignore`, unless the folder is already inside a repository:

```{.text filename="Project layout"}
hello/
  .gitignore
  Cargo.toml
  src/
    main.rs
```

The `Cargo.toml` file describes the project, much as `DESCRIPTION` describes an R package (@sec-crates covers it):

```{.toml filename="Cargo.toml"}
[package]
name = "hello"
version = "0.1.0"
edition = "2024"

[dependencies]
```

The file `src/main.rs` holds the program. Cargo starts you off with this one:

```{rust}
#| label: rust-hello
#| filename: src/main.rs
fn main() {
    println!("Hello, world!");
}
```

Every Rust program starts running at `fn main()`. Rust's `println!` prints a line; the `!` marks it as a macro rather than a function, a distinction @sec-macros explains. To compile and run the program, use `cargo run` from inside the project folder:

```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
cargo run
```

Cargo reports what it did, then the program's output appears:

```{.text filename="Terminal"}
   Compiling hello v0.1.0 (/path/to/hello)
    Finished `dev` profile [unoptimized + debuginfo] target(s) in 0.44s
     Running `target/debug/hello`
Hello, world!
```

The compiled program is now in `target/debug/hello`, and you could run it directly. The `dev` profile is a debug build, which compiles quickly and checks for mistakes such as integer overflow (@sec-types). A few other commands come up often:

| Command | What it does | Closest R equivalent |
|-------------------|------------------------------|-------------------|
| `cargo run` | Compile, then run | `Rscript script.R` |
| `cargo check` | Report errors without building a program, which is faster | None; R reports errors as it runs |
| `cargo build --release` | Build an optimized program in `target/release/` | None |
| `cargo fmt` | Reformat the code | `styler::style_file()` |
| `cargo clippy` | Flag common mistakes and unidiomatic code | `lintr::lint()` |

Many examples in this book leave out `fn main()` to stay short. To run one yourself, paste it between the braces of `fn main() { }` in `src/main.rs`.

## The syntax you need for now

Most of Rust's basic syntax has a direct counterpart in R. This section covers the pieces @sec-vectors and @sec-types use, each next to its R counterpart.

### Variables and printing

R assigns with `<-` by convention. The `=` sign works too, except inside a function call, where it names an argument instead. Rust uses `let`, and each statement ends with a semicolon:

```{r}
#| label: r-variables
x <- 5
cat("x is", x, "\n")
```

```{rust}
#| label: rust-variables
let x = 5;
println!("x is {x}");
println!("x is {}", x);
```

In Rust, `println!` fills each pair of braces with a value. You can name a variable inside the braces, as in `{x}`, or leave the braces empty and pass the value after the string. @sec-vectors adds a third form, `{:?}`, for values such as vectors.

The compiler works out that `x` is an integer. You can also state the type, as in `let x: i32 = 5;`, where `i32` is a 32-bit integer. @sec-types covers the number types.

### Variables don't change unless you say so

In R, any variable can be reassigned. In Rust, a variable can't be, unless you declare it with `mut`:

```{rust}
#| label: rust-immutable
#| error: true
let max_iter = 100;
max_iter = 200;
println!("{max_iter}");
```

The compiler points at both lines and suggests the fix:

```{rust}
#| label: rust-mutable
let mut max_iter = 100;
max_iter = 200;
println!("{max_iter}");
```

::: {.callout-tip title="The same idea in R"}
R can lock a variable too, but you have to ask. Here, `lockBinding()` locks the name `max_iter` in `environment()`, the environment the code runs in:

```{r}
#| label: r-lock-binding
#| error: true
max_iter <- 100
lockBinding("max_iter", environment())
max_iter <- 200
```

Rust reverses the default. Variables are locked unless you opt out with `mut`, so a `let` without `mut` tells the reader the value won't change.
:::

### Statements, expressions, and semicolons

In R, a newline ends an expression once it's complete, and a semicolon is only needed to put two expressions on one line. In Rust, the semicolon isn't optional punctuation: whether a line ends with one changes what it means. Rust separates two kinds of code:

- An *expression* produces a value: `5`, `x + 1`, or a function call.
- A *statement* does something and produces no value. A `let` is a statement, and so is any expression followed by a semicolon: the semicolon runs the expression and discards its value. That's why every `println!` in this chapter ends with one.

R has no statements at all. Even assignment is an expression, which is why `y <- (x <- 5)` works. A Rust `let` has no value, so it can't appear inside another expression.

The difference matters most inside braces. A block, `{ ... }`, is an expression, and its value is its last expression, written without a semicolon. R's braces work the same way:

```{r}
#| label: r-block
x <- 3
y <- {
  doubled <- x * 2
  doubled + 1
}
y
```

```{rust}
#| label: rust-block
let x = 3;
let y = {
    let doubled = x * 2;
    doubled + 1
};
println!("{y}");
```

Inside the braces, `let doubled = x * 2;` is a statement and `doubled + 1` is the block's value. The semicolon after the closing brace ends the outer `let`. In practice, three rules cover nearly every case:

- End each `let`, and each line that only does something (such as a `println!`), with a semicolon.
- Leave the semicolon off the last line of a block when that line is the value the block should produce. That's how a function returns a value and how an `if` produces one.
- The closing brace of a function definition, a `for` loop, or an `if` that stands on its own needs no semicolon. A `let` whose value is a block or an `if` still ends with one, because the `let` is a statement.

::: {.callout-warning title="Where the analogy breaks"}
R's braces group code but don't limit where a name exists, so after the R block, `doubled` is still defined and holds 6. Rust's braces do limit it. The block hands its value to `y`, but `doubled` exists only inside it. Using `doubled` after the closing brace is a compile error: "cannot find value `doubled` in this scope". A `for` loop's variable is limited the same way: it doesn't exist after the loop.
:::

### Functions

Here's the same function in R and in Rust. The Rust one lists the type of each argument and of the value it returns:

```{r}
#| label: r-function
add <- function(x, y) {
  x + y
}
add(2, 3)
```

```{rust}
#| label: rust-function
fn add(x: i32, y: i32) -> i32 {
    x + y
}

fn main() {
    println!("{}", add(2, 3));
}
```

The `-> i32` after the arguments is the return type. Both languages return the value of the last expression in the body, so neither needs an explicit `return`. Functions usually go outside `main()`, so most examples that define one show `main()` as well.

::: {.callout-warning title="Where the analogy breaks"}
In R, `function(x, y) { x + y; }` still returns the sum. In Rust, a function body is a block, so the rule from the previous section applies: the last expression must not end with a semicolon. With one, it becomes a statement, the function returns nothing (written `()` in the error), and the compiler objects:

```{rust}
#| label: rust-semicolon
#| error: true
fn add(x: i32, y: i32) -> i32 {
    x + y;
}

fn main() {
    println!("{}", add(2, 3));
}
```
:::

### `if` and `else`

In both languages `if` is an expression, so it can produce a value:

```{r}
#| label: r-if
x <- -2
sign <- if (x > 0) "positive" else "not positive"
sign
```

```{rust}
#| label: rust-if
let x = -2;
let sign = if x > 0 { "positive" } else { "not positive" };
println!("{sign}");
```

Rust drops the parentheses around the condition and requires the braces. Each branch is a block whose value is its last expression, so `"positive"` and `"not positive"` have no semicolons; the `let` around the whole `if` does. The condition must be a `bool`: R accepts `if (1)`, but Rust rejects `if 1` because a number isn't a true or false value. The two branches must also produce the same type. Both produce text here, and replacing either string with `0` is a compile error, even for a branch that never runs. R lets each branch return whatever it likes. @sec-types has more on how strictly Rust keeps types apart.

### `for` loops

A loop over a range looks almost the same in both languages:

```{r}
#| label: r-for
for (i in 1:3) {
  cat("step", i, "\n")
}
```

```{rust}
#| label: rust-for
for i in 1..=3 {
    println!("step {i}");
}
```

In Rust, `1..=3` runs from 1 to 3, like R's `1:3`. Without the `=`, a range stops before its end: `1..3` covers 1 and 2. @sec-vectors uses that second form to take part of a vector.

::: {.callout-warning title="Where the analogy breaks"}
R's `3:1` counts down. A Rust range only counts up, so `3..=1` is empty, and a loop over it runs zero times without any error. To count down, reverse the range with `(1..=3).rev()`; @sec-iterators covers methods like this one.
:::

### Comments

R comments start with `#`; Rust comments start with `//`. Rust also has documentation comments that start with `///`, the counterpart of roxygen's `#'` (@sec-crates).

## Summary

| R | Rust |
|---------------------------|---------------------------|
| Type at the console | Write `src/main.rs`, then `cargo run` |
| `x <- 5` | `let x = 5;` |
| A newline ends a complete expression | A semicolon ends a statement |
| `{ ... }` evaluates to its last expression | A block's value is its last expression, without a semicolon |
| Any variable can be reassigned | `let mut x = 5;` to allow it |
| `cat("x is", x, "\n")` | `println!("x is {x}");` |
| `function(x, y) x + y` | `fn add(x: i32, y: i32) -> i32 { x + y }` |
| `if (x > 0) a else b` | `if x > 0 { a } else { b }` |
| `for (i in 1:3)` | `for i in 1..=3` |
| `# comment` | `// comment` |
